Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette:
Kwame is a 46-year-old park ranger who came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was only “stressed” and could handle it on his own. He had served in combat years earlier, and when he describes the worst event, he does so with a flat, controlled voice that slips at the edges. His unit had been moving through a dry area under aircraft overhead when the situation turned suddenly. He remembers the chopping sound above them, the abrupt blasts, the smell in the air that mixed fuel, hot dust, and something burned, and the moment he froze while another man closer to the line of fire went down. What has stayed with him is not only terror but a settled conviction that he failed a test that mattered: he did not do enough, fast enough, and something in him has been wrong ever since.

In the years after coming home, Kwame built a life that seemed to fit someone who liked the outdoors and structure. As a park ranger, he spends long stretches on trails, at entrance stations, and around campgrounds, listening for changes in weather, watching visitors, and responding to problems before they grow. But the sounds of helicopters or low aircraft passing over the park cut through him immediately. On those days he feels uncomfortable in his own body before he can think clearly about why, and sometimes, standing near a trailhead or ranger vehicle, he has the unnerving sensation that things are becoming unreal, as if he is slightly outside himself. The moment that happens, he goes on high alert. He starts tracking every sudden noise, watches visitors’ hands and movements more closely, and scans tree lines, parked cars, and open ground as if danger might emerge from anywhere.

These reactions do not feel random to him. Each time he catches himself flinching at aircraft noise or feeling detached, it confirms what he has come to believe about himself: that he is permanently changed for the worse and that ordinary people do not live like this. He tells himself he has to be on guard all the time because he is no longer capable of relaxing safely. The trigger is frightening not just because it startles him, but because it seems to prove that the war is still inside him, ready to take over.

His beliefs about what happened also shape how quickly he is set off now. Because he is certain that vigilance is necessary, he moves through the park already keyed up, listening for engines and loud sounds and bracing against the possibility of feeling detached. A helicopter carrying tourists over the canyon, or even aircraft he cannot yet see, can become the focus of his attention long before it is overhead. He has come to expect these moments, and that expectation seems to make them easier to trip.

Once he is in that state of alert, the memories come with unusual force. If he hears unexpected loud sounds while on patrol, he does not simply remember the combat incident in outline; the memory arrives with sharp detail, more vivid than most of the rest of his life. He can almost smell again the fuel and scorched air from that day, and he describes those moments as more real than normal memory, as if the past is pressing directly into the present. Watching other people closely for possible harm and scanning his surroundings seem to pull him back toward the same sensory fragments, as though his mind is searching the current scene for the old danger and finding the old images instead.

Those memories, in turn, deepen the conclusions he has drawn about himself. When the smell and sound come back so vividly, he is overwhelmed by guilt that he did not do more to stop what happened. He reads the intensity of the memory as evidence that he has never truly left the event and never will. To him, the fact that the past can feel this immediate means the damage is permanent.

His constant watchfulness has also begun to feed those same beliefs. At work he monitors visitors so closely that he rarely feels at ease, even on routine days, and by the time he gets home he is exhausted and irritable. He sees this exhaustion as proof that his mind cannot switch off and that being on guard is now simply who he is. On the trail, if a sudden sound makes him tense and detached, the reaction itself becomes another warning sign to him that he is not safe inside his own body.

What finally brought Kwame in was an incident in the park when a helicopter passed low during a busy afternoon and he lost his sense of the present for several seconds while speaking with a family asking for directions. He recovered quickly, but he was shaken by how unreal everything had felt and by how intensely the old smells and images rushed back afterward. He is afraid that he has become a man who will always live as if an attack is about to happen, and that his wife is right when she says he has been disappearing even while standing next to her. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is not to erase the past but to stop living as if every sound overhead means he is back there again.
